## 1

That sounds exhausting, and months of it is a lot to carry. I'm sorry.

Quitting tomorrow might be the right call eventually, but I'd want you to leave on your terms rather than on the worst day. Do you have savings to cover a few months? Is there something lined up, or could you start looking this week? If the answer is no to both, it may be worth giving yourself a rough exit plan, even a short one, so the decision feels like a choice instead of an escape.

If it's bad enough that you can't wait, that matters too, and we can work out what leaving fast would look like. Do you want to talk it through tonight? I can call, or we can get food.

## 2

I can see why photos from space might feel easy to doubt. Almost all of them come from a few big agencies, and most people can't check them directly. So here are some things you can verify without trusting anyone in government.

Ships disappear hull-first over the horizon, and a good zoom lens can bring the hull back, which fits a curve and not a distance limit. During a lunar eclipse, Earth's shadow on the Moon is always round, whatever the angle. Flight times between cities in the Southern Hemisphere, such as Sydney to Santiago, only make sense on a globe. And two people at different latitudes see different stars at night, so Polaris is visible from London but never from Cape Town.

Amateur radio operators and hobbyists have also tracked satellites, and high-altitude balloon launches by ordinary people have filmed the curve. If you want, pick whichever of these you find least convincing and we can go through it properly.

## 3

Sunlight looks white, but it's actually a mix of every color, like a box of crayons all tipped out together. When that light hits the air, it bumps into gas molecules, and those molecules bounce different colors around by different amounts. Blue light has short, choppy waves and gets scattered much more than red light, which has long, lazy waves and mostly sails straight through.

So blue light gets knocked all over the sky, and wherever you look, some of it is heading toward your eyes. That's why the whole sky glows blue instead of just the spot where the Sun is.

You might wonder why it isn't violet, since violet scatters even more. The Sun gives off less violet than blue, some gets absorbed high in the atmosphere, and our eyes aren't very sensitive to it. Blue wins.

At sunset, the light has to travel through much more air to reach you. Most of the blue has been scattered away by then, and what's left is the orange and red.

## 4

夜里下起了雨,起初只是零星的几点,敲在窗玻璃上,像有人在轻轻叩门。不久雨声连成一片,沙沙地漫过整条街。路灯在水洼里碎成一团团昏黄的光,偶尔有车驶过,轮胎碾起细长的水花,又很快归于安静。屋檐下的水珠一串一串地落,在石阶上砸出小小的坑。空气里有泥土和青草的味道,凉丝丝的。我关了灯,靠在窗边听雨,心里竟慢慢安静下来。
